Upper and Lower Sums Close In

Rectangles pack the region under a curve to measure its area. Lower and upper sums squeeze the true area from both sides.

The answer sits between the underfilled and overfilled totals. Finer partitions narrow the gap between them. When the gap vanishes, that value is the integral.

For example, fit square pieces into the curved shape of a 🍰 cake. The smaller you cut the pieces, the fewer gaps remain and the better they match.

L(f,P)≤∫abf≤U(f,P)L(f,P) \le \int_a^b f \le U(f,P)L(f,P)≤∫ab​f≤U(f,P)

Prove the Dirichlet function is not Riemann integrable by showing U−L=1U - L = 1U−L=1 for every partition.

U(D,P)=1,L(D,P)=0for every PU(D,P) = 1, \quad L(D,P) = 0 \quad \text{for every } PU(D,P)=1,L(D,P)=0for every P
Show proof

  1. Every interval contains both rationals and irrationals, so on every subinterval sup⁡D=1\sup D = 1supD=1 and inf⁡D=0\inf D = 0infD=0.

  2. Hence for every partition PPP, U(D,P)=∑1⋅Δxk=1U(D,P) = \sum 1\cdot\Delta x_k = 1U(D,P)=∑1⋅Δxk​=1 and L(D,P)=∑0⋅Δxk=0L(D,P) = \sum 0\cdot\Delta x_k = 0L(D,P)=∑0⋅Δxk​=0.

  3. Since U−L=1↛0U - L = 1 \not\to 0U−L=1→0, the necessary and sufficient condition for Riemann integrability fails.

Prove that refining a partition never increases U−LU - LU−L.

P′⊃P  ⇒  U(f,P′)≤U(f,P),  L(f,P′)≥L(f,P)P' \supset P \;\Rightarrow\; U(f,P') \le U(f,P),\; L(f,P') \ge L(f,P)P′⊃P⇒U(f,P′)≤U(f,P),L(f,P′)≥L(f,P)
Show proof

  1. Splitting one subinterval in two: each piece's supremum is at most the original's, so the upper sum decreases (or stays).

  2. Likewise each piece's infimum is at least the original's, so the lower sum increases (or stays).

  3. So U−LU - LU−L decreases monotonically under refinement — the sums squeeze toward each other.
